references.text: Parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says exactly the same thing: 'The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask therefore the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.' This is the closest parallel to Luke 10:2.

Jesus uses the harvest metaphor in conversation with the disciples at Jacob's well: 'Lift up your eyes and look at the fields, they are already white for harvest!' He sends them out to harvest where others have sown, complementing the image of the great harvest.

Joel uses the harvest image eschatologically: 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe!' The image of a great harvest waiting for workers has roots in Old Testament prophetic language about God's judgment and gathering.
Proverbs speaks of the one who gathers in summer as a wise son, while the one who sleeps during harvest brings shame. This underscores the urgency of the harvest—the workers must not be few or late.
The immediate context: Jesus appointed seventy(-two) others and sent them out two by two ahead of him to every town and place where he himself was about to go. Verse 2 is the reason for this sending.

Background for the harvest saying in Matthew: Jesus saw the crowds and had compassion on them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. This shows the motivation behind the prayer for more workers.

Paul uses an agricultural metaphor about missionary work: 'I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth … we are God's fellow workers; you are God's field.' The workers in the harvest is a recurring image for servants of the gospel.
Jesus sent out the twelve two by two and gave them authority over unclean spirits. Parallel to the sending in Luke 10, where more workers are sent out into the harvest.

Paul urges Timothy to be 'a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.' The term 'worker' (ἐργάτης) is directly linked to service in God's kingdom, just as Jesus uses it in Luke 10:2.

Ruth's harvest scene is a background for the harvest metaphor: Ruth asks to glean among the sheaves after the harvesters. The image of harvesting people builds on the rich Old Testament harvest tradition.
